Catherine of Alexandria

Icons

Saints

St. Catherine of Alexandria

Katherine · Aikaterina

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

Scripture

1Corinthians1:27–29

King James Version · Scripture previews

Saint Catherine’s parish explains the saint’s imperial garments, martyr’s cross, books, celestial sphere, and wheel as identifying attributes in her iconography.

[1] Published source,paragraph 11

What is depicted

The selected historic Sinai icon shows Catherine enthroned with books, instruments, and narrative scenes. Its whole composition is retained, including the surrounding episodes; it is not cropped to conceal contextual details.

[2] Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field title; Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.ImageDescription; Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.Artist; Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.Credit; Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.LicenseShortName

History and tradition

The parish’s published life recounts Catherine’s learned defense of Christianity and her martyrdom, then connects her relics with the Sinai monastery. These are its hagiographic traditions. The selected icon is an illustration of her later veneration, not a contemporary record of the trial.

[1] Published source,paragraph 5; Published source,paragraph 6; Published source,paragraph 7; Published source,paragraph 8; Published source,paragraph 9 · [2] Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field title; Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.ImageDescription; Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.Artist; Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.Credit; Exact file record File:Icon of Saint Catherine.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.LicenseShortName

Published explanation

The parish explicitly associates the books and celestial sphere with knowledge and wisdom, and the wheel with martyrdom. Its explanation of her courtly clothing belongs to that published iconographic reading. The symbols are attributed to the parish rather than invented for the app.

[1] Published source,paragraph 11

But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;

And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are:

That no flesh should glory in his presence.

Related Scripture; not an invented quotation spoken by Catherine.

[3] 1Cor 1:27–29
